claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 are abundant proteins that shuttle between the cytoplasm and membrane to modulate multiple cellular processes, including cytoskeletal dynamics, proliferation, and secretion.
source: Marcks and Marcksl1 are abundant proteins that shuttle between the cytoplasm and membrane to modulate multiple cellular processes, including cytoskeletal dynamics, proliferation, and secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 have partly redundant functions and are required for normal neurite formation during embryonic spinal cord development.
source: We show that Marcks and Marcksl1 have partly redundant functions and are required for normal neurite formation and proliferation of neuro-glial progenitors during embryonic spinal cord development and for its regeneration during tadpole stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 are required for proliferation of neuro-glial progenitors during embryonic spinal cord development.
source: We show that Marcks and Marcksl1 have partly redundant functions and are required for normal neurite formation and proliferation of neuro-glial progenitors during embryonic spinal cord development and for its regeneration during tadpole stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 are required for spinal cord regeneration during tadpole stages.
source: We show that Marcks and Marcksl1 have partly redundant functions and are required for normal neurite formation and proliferation of neuro-glial progenitors during embryonic spinal cord development and for its regeneration during tadpole stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Some functions of Marcks and Marcksl1 in the spinal cord are mediated by phospholipid signaling.
source: Rescue experiments in Marcks and Marcksl1 loss-of-function animals further suggested that some of the functions of Marcks and Marcksl1 in the spinal cord are mediated by phospholipid signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological rescue experiments in the results section.

claim: Spinal cord injury in humans is a life-changing condition with no effective treatment.
source: Spinal cord injury (SCI) in humans is a life-changing condition with no effective treatment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Many non-mammalian vertebrates can fully regenerate their spinal cords after injury.
source: However, many non-mammalian vertebrates can fully regenerate their spinal cords after injury (Lee-Liu et al., 2013; Alunni and Bally-Cuif, 2016; Rodemer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Xenopus tadpoles can fully regenerate the spinal cord.
source: In the clawed toad Xenopus, tadpoles can fully regenerate the spinal cord; however, this capacity is lost during metamorphosis (Beattie et al., 1990; Gibbs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The capacity for spinal cord regeneration is lost during metamorphosis in Xenopus.
source: In the clawed toad Xenopus, tadpoles can fully regenerate the spinal cord; however, this capacity is lost during metamorphosis (Beattie et al., 1990; Gibbs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 were identified as highly upregulated at the tadpole stage but downregulated in froglets after spinal cord injury in a proteomic screen.
source: A recent proteomic screen to identify proteins differentially regulated in regeneration-competent tadpoles versus regeneration-incompetent froglets after SCI identified a number of proteins that are highly upregulated at the tadpole stage but downregulated in froglets (Kshirsagar, 2020). These proteins included Marcks and Marcksl1, which had previously been implicated in the regeneration of other tissues (El Amri et al., 2018) suggesting a potential role for these proteins also in spinal cord regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Marcks has three highly conserved functional domains: an effector domain (ED), a Marcks Homology 2 (MH2) domain, and a myristoylation domain.
source: Marcks is an abundant and widely expressed protein with three highly conserved functional domains: an effector domain (ED), a Marcks Homology 2 (MH2) domain, and a myristoylation domain (Brudvig and Weimer, 2015; El Amri et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcksl1 shares strong homology and functionality with Marcks.
source: Marcks-like protein 1 (Marcksl1) shares strong homology and functionality with Marcks (Stumpo et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In an unphosphorylated state, the positively charged ED of Marcks attaches to the plasma membrane, and the myristoylation site tethers the protein to the membrane.
source: In an unphosphorylated state, the positively charged ED of Marcks attaches to the plasma membrane, and the myristoylation site tethers the protein to the membrane (Kim et al., 1994; McLaughlin and Aderem, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When the ED is phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC), Marcks translocates to the cytoplasm.
source: However, when the ED is phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC), thereby acquiring more negative charges, Marcks translocates to the cytoplasm (Brudvig and Weimer, 2015; McLaughlin and Aderem, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 modulate the polymerization and cross-linking of actin filaments.
source: For example, they have been shown to modulate the polymerization and cross-linking of actin filaments, recruit secretory vesicles to the membrane, and interact with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), thereby regulating multiple signaling pathways downstream of PIP2 such as phospholipase C (PLC) and phospholipase D (PLD) dependent pathways (Hartwig et al., 1992; Morash et al., 1998; Yarmola et al., 2001; Wohnsland et al., 2000; McLaughlin et al., 2002; Sundaram et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 recruit secretory vesicles to the membrane.
source: For example, they have been shown to modulate the polymerization and cross-linking of actin filaments, recruit secretory vesicles to the membrane, and interact with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), thereby regulating multiple signaling pathways downstream of PIP2 such as phospholipase C (PLC) and phospholipase D (PLD) dependent pathways (Hartwig et al., 1992; Morash et al., 1998; Yarmola et al., 2001; Wohnsland et al., 2000; McLaughlin et al., 2002; Sundaram et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 interact with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: For example, they have been shown to modulate the polymerization and cross-linking of actin filaments, recruit secretory vesicles to the membrane, and interact with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), thereby regulating multiple signaling pathways downstream of PIP2 such as phospholipase C (PLC) and phospholipase D (PLD) dependent pathways (Hartwig et al., 1992; Morash et al., 1998; Yarmola et al., 2001; Wohnsland et al., 2000; McLaughlin et al., 2002; Sundaram et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 regulate multiple signaling pathways downstream of PIP2 such as phospholipase C (PLC) and phospholipase D (PLD) dependent pathways.
source: For example, they have been shown to modulate the polymerization and cross-linking of actin filaments, recruit secretory vesicles to the membrane, and interact with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), thereby regulating multiple signaling pathways downstream of PIP2 such as phospholipase C (PLC) and phospholipase D (PLD) dependent pathways (Hartwig et al., 1992; Morash et al., 1998; Yarmola et al., 2001; Wohnsland et al., 2000; McLaughlin et al., 2002; Sundaram et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 affect cytoskeletal dynamics, cell migration, secretion, cell proliferation, and differentiation in the nervous system and other tissues.
source: Consequently, Marcks and Marcksl1 affect cytoskeletal dynamics, cell migration, secretion, cell proliferation, and differentiation in the nervous system and other tissues (Brudvig and Weimer, 2015; El Amri et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 proteins were found to be upregulated in several different regenerative processes, such as lens regeneration in newts, fin regeneration in lungfish and bichirs, tail regeneration in lizards, and cardiac tissue regeneration following infarction in mice.
source: Importantly, Marcks and Marcksl1 proteins were found to be upregulated in several different regenerative processes, such as lens regeneration in newts, fin regeneration in lungfish and bichirs, tail regeneration in lizards, and cardiac tissue regeneration following infarction in mice (Bock-Marquette et al., 2009; Sousounis et al., 2014; Nogueira et al., 2016; Alibardi, 2017; Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A Marcks-like protein in axolotls (AxMLP) initiates an early proliferative response in axolotl tail and limb regeneration.
source: Moreover, a Marcks-like protein in axolotls (AxMLP) initiates an early proliferative response in axolotl tail and limb regeneration (Sugiura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 are significantly upregulated in outgrowing and/or regenerating neurites of facial motor neurons, dorsal root, and superior cervical ganglia, in the optic nerve and during axonal sprouting after brain stroke.
source: In the nervous system, Marcks and Marcksl1 are also significantly upregulated in outgrowing and/or regenerating neurites of facial motor neurons, dorsal root, and superior cervical ganglia, in the optic nerve and during axonal sprouting after brain stroke, suggesting an essential role for Marcks and Marcksl1 in neurite outgrowth and regeneration in both the peripheral and central nervous systems (McNamara et al., 2000; Carmichael et al., 2005; Szpara et al., 2007; Veldman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: marcks.S, marcksl1.S, and marcksl1.L are expressed in the brain and spinal cord as well as in the pharyngeal arches, somites, intermediate mesoderm, and blood islands of the ventrolateral mesoderm in Xenopus embryos.
source: They are expressed in the brain and spinal cord as well as in the pharyngeal arches, somites, intermediate mesoderm, and blood islands of the ventrolateral mesoderm confirming previous reports (Gawantka et al., 1998; Zhao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: marcks.S is more broadly distributed through the entire brain, whereas marcksl1.L and marcksl1.S have a more restricted expression and are absent from the forebrain.
source: marcks.S is more broadly distributed through the entire brain, whereas marcksl1.L and marcksl1.S have a more restricted expression and are absent from the forebrain.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Marcks and Marcksl1 are mostly associated with outer cell membranes in the ventricular zone and the adjacent mantle zone of the developing spinal cord at stage 26.
source: Confocal microscopy of embryos injected with mRNAs encoding a membrane-tethered form of GFP (memGFP) and transversely sectioned at stage 26 revealed that Marcks and Marcksl1 are mostly associated with outer cell membranes. This is true for the ventricular zone, where progenitor cells are located, and the adjacent mantle zone, which harbors migrating and differentiating neurons (Figure 1K–P, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1K-P.

claim: A subset of cells in both ventricular and mantle zones shows cytoplasmic expression of Marcks and Marcksl1.
source: In addition, a subset of cells in both ventricular and mantle zones shows cytoplasmic expression of Marcks and Marcksl1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1K-P.

claim: Marcks, but not Marcksl1 was also occasionally seen in cell nuclei.
source: Marcks, but not Marcksl1 was also occasionally seen in cell nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1K-P.

claim: Individual knockdown of marcks or marcksl1 did not lead to significant alterations in immunostaining for the neurite marker acetylated tubulin in stage 34 embryos compared to an unspecific control MO.
source: None of these injections led to significant alterations in immunostaining for the neurite marker acetylated tubulin on the injected side of the spinal cord relative to the uninjected side in stage 34 embryos compared to an unspecific control MO (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Co-injection of MOs targeting all four homeologs (marcks.S/L, marcksl1.S, and marcksl1.L) significantly decreased acetylated tubulin staining on the injected side.
source: However, when the three MOs targeting marcks.S/L, marcksl1.S, and marcksl1.L were co-injected, thus blocking all four homeologs (4M MO), acetylated tubulin staining was significantly decreased on the injected side (Figure 2D, E, G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D, E, G.

claim: Co-injection of mRNA constructs encoding chicken Marcks and Xenopus tropicalis Marcksl1 resulted in complete rescue of acetylated tubulin staining in 4M MO embryos.
source: Co-injection of mRNA constructs encoding chicken Marcks and Xenopus tropicalis Marcksl1, which were selectively mutated to prevent MO binding, resulted in complete rescue of acetylated tubulin staining, confirming the specific action of the MOs used (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F, G.

claim: Unilateral CRISPR-mediated knockout of all Marcks and Marcksl1 homeologs (4M CRISPR) led to a significant reduction in acetylated tubulin staining on the injected side compared to Cas9 and slc45a2 controls.
source: Similar to the knockdown of the proteins by MOs, the unilateral CRISPR-mediated knockout of all Marcks and Marcksl1 homeologs (4M CRISPR) led to a significant reduction in acetylated tubulin staining on the injected side compared to Cas9 and slc45a2 controls (Figure 2H–K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2H-K.

claim: Overexpression of both marcks and marcksl1 by injection of mRNA resulted in a significant increase in acetylated tubulin staining on the injected side compared to control embryos.
source: Conversely, overexpression of both proteins by injection of marcks and marcksl1 mRNA at two different doses (100 or 300 pg each) together with myc-GFP mRNA resulted in a significant increase in acetylated tubulin staining on the injected side compared to that in control embryos injected with myc-GFP mRNA alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The proportion of PH3-positive ventricular nuclei on the injected side was significantly reduced in both 4M MO and 4M CRISPR embryos compared to control injections.
source: The proportion of PH3-positive ventricular nuclei on the injected side (expressed as the ratio between injected/uninjected sides) was significantly reduced in both experiments compared to control injections (Figure 3A–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A-H.

claim: Injection of marcks and marcksl1 mRNA resulted in a significant increase in the proportion of PH3-positive ventricular nuclei on the injected side compared to control embryos.
source: Conversely, the injection of marcks and marcksl1 mRNA together with myc-GFP mRNA resulted in a significant increase in the proportion of PH3-positive ventricular nuclei on the injected side compared to control embryos injected with myc-GFP mRNA alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of Sox2- or Sox3-positive nuclei on the injected side was significantly reduced in 4M CRISPR embryos compared to control embryos.
source: The number of Sox2- or Sox3-positive nuclei on the injected side (expressed as a ratio between injected/uninjected sides) was significantly reduced as compared to control embryos injected with slc45a2 sgRNAs or with Cas9 alone (Figure 3I–M).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3I-M.

claim: Overall cell numbers (as indicated by the numbers of DAPI+ nuclei) on the injected side were not significantly reduced in 4M MO or 4M CRISPR embryos.
source: In spite of the reduction in progenitor proliferation after Marcks/Marcksl1 loss of function, overall cell numbers (as indicated by the numbers of DAPI+ nuclei) on the injected side were not yet significantly reduced in these embryos (Figure 3N, O) indicating that the decrease in neurite staining described in the previous section cannot be attributed to a reduction in overall cell number.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3N, O.

claim: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) significantly increased the intensity of acetylated tubulin staining on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: Compared to DMSO-treated controls, incubation in the phospholipid signaling activator S1P significantly increased the intensity of acetylated tubulin staining (Figure 4A) as well as the proportion of PH3-positive cells (Figure 4B) on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side suggesting that Marcks and Marcksl1 promote neurite outgrowth and progenitor proliferation at least partly by a phospholipid-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) significantly increased the proportion of PH3-positive cells on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: Compared to DMSO-treated controls, incubation in the phospholipid signaling activator S1P significantly increased the intensity of acetylated tubulin staining (Figure 4A) as well as the proportion of PH3-positive cells (Figure 4B) on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side suggesting that Marcks and Marcksl1 promote neurite outgrowth and progenitor proliferation at least partly by a phospholipid-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M-3M3FBS, which specifically activates PLC-dependent phospholipid signaling, significantly increased the proportion of PH3-positive cells but not acetylated tubulin in 4M CRISPR embryos compared to controls.
source: However, after incubation in the compound M-3M3FBS, which specifically activates PLC-dependent phospholipid signaling (Bae et al., 2003), only the proportion of PH3-positive cells was significantly increased compared to the controls (Figure 4D), but acetylated tubulin was not (Figure 4C), suggesting that PLC signaling may mediate some of the effects of Marcks and Marcksl1 on progenitor proliferation but not on neurite formation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: The specific PLD inhibitor FIPI had no significant effect on neurite formation or progenitor proliferation in Marcks/Marcksl1-depleted spinal cords during development.
source: In contrast, neither the specific PLD inhibitor FIPI (Monovich et al., 2007; Su et al., 2009), nor the specific PLC inhibitor U-73122 (Bleasdale et al., 1989) had any significant effect on neurite formation or progenitor proliferation in Marcks/Marcksl1-depleted spinal cords (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The specific PLC inhibitor U-73122 had no significant effect on neurite formation or progenitor proliferation in Marcks/Marcksl1-depleted spinal cords during development.
source: In contrast, neither the specific PLD inhibitor FIPI (Monovich et al., 2007; Su et al., 2009), nor the specific PLC inhibitor U-73122 (Bleasdale et al., 1989) had any significant effect on neurite formation or progenitor proliferation in Marcks/Marcksl1-depleted spinal cords (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: N-methyllidocaine iodide (NMI), which enhances PIP2 biosynthesis, showed a significant increase in the intensity of acetylated tubulin staining and in the proportion of PH3-positive cells on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: Compared to DMSO-treated controls, embryos in which NMI enhanced PIP2 biosynthesis showed a significant increase in the intensity of acetylated tubulin staining (Figure 4E) as well as in the proportion of PH3-positive cells (Figure 4F) on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: The PIP2 synthesis inhibitor ISA-2011B had no significant effect on neurite formation or progenitor proliferation in Marcks/Marcksl1-depleted spinal cords during development.
source: In contrast, the PIP2 synthesis inhibitor ISA-2011B had no significant effect (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: The PKC inhibitor Go6983 showed a significant increase in the intensity of acetylated tubulin staining and in the proportion of PH3-positive cells on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: Compared to DMSO-treated controls, embryos treated with the PKC inhibitor Go6983 showed a significant increase in the intensity of acetylated tubulin staining (Figure 4G) as well as in the proportion of PH3-positive cells (Figure 4H) on the CRISPR-injected side relative to the uninjected side.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G, H.

claim: The PKC activator PMA had no significant effect on neurite formation or progenitor proliferation in Marcks/Marcksl1-depleted spinal cords during development.
source: In contrast, the PKC activator PMA had no significant effect (Figure 4G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G, H.

claim: Marcks protein was detected primarily in the meningeal layer surrounding the spinal cord, with relatively little immunostaining in the spinal cord itself in uninjected, uninjured tadpoles.
source: In uninjected, uninjured tadpoles, Marcks protein was detected primarily in the meningeal layer surrounding the spinal cord, with relatively little immunostaining in the spinal cord itself (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Barely any Marcks protein was detectable in uninjured 4M CRISPR tadpoles.
source: Barely any Marcks protein was detectable in uninjured 4M CRISPR tadpoles (Figure 5N, O).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5N, O.

claim: At 5 DPT, normal tadpoles showed an apparent upregulation of Marcks in all layers of the spinal cord adjacent to the injury site, including the ventricular zone, the mantle zone, and the marginal zone.
source: At 5 DPT, normal tadpoles showed an apparent upregulation of Marcks in all layers of the spinal cord adjacent to the injury site, including the ventricular zone, where neuro-glial progenitors reside, the mantle zone, which harbors differentiated neurons, and the marginal zone, occupied by neurites (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: Marcks continues to be elevated in cells in the region of the injury gap at 5 DPT.
source: Marcks also continues to be elevated in cells in the region of the injury gap, which is about to close (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: The pattern of elevated Marcks staining was maintained at 10 DPT.
source: This pattern of elevated Marcks staining was maintained at 10 DPT (Figure 5K–M, V).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5K-M, V.

claim: 4M CRISPR tadpoles showed no significant increases of Marcks immunostaining in the spinal cord or adjacent tissues at 5- and 10-DPT.
source: In contrast, 4M CRISPR tadpoles showed no significant increases of Marcks immunostaining in the spinal cord or adjacent tissues at 5- and 10-DPT (Figure 5R–U).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5R-U.

claim: Marcksl1 showed slightly stronger immunostaining in the spinal cord and weaker staining in the meninges of uninjected uninjured tadpoles compared to Marcks.
source: Compared to Marcks, Marcksl1 showed slightly stronger immunostaining in the spinal cord and weaker staining in the meninges of uninjected uninjured tadpoles but less pronounced upregulation after SCI (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–L, U).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-L, U.

claim: Marcksl1-immunopositive cells accumulated within the injury gap from 2 DPT onwards.
source: As described for Marcks, Marcksl1-immunopositive cells also accumulated within the injury gap from 2 DPT onwards (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–L).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-L.

claim: Almost no Marcksl1 immunostaining was detectable in 4M CRISPR tadpoles in and around the spinal cord before the injury, and no significant changes were observed following SCI.
source: Again, almost no Marcksl1 immunostaining was detectable in 4M CRISPR tadpoles in and around the spinal cord before the injury, and no significant changes were observed following SCI (Figure 5—figure supplement 1M–T, U).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1M-T, U.

claim: The distances covered by uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected uninjured tadpoles were not significantly different.
source: The distances covered by uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected uninjured tadpoles were not significantly different (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by swimming test data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Following SCI, there is a significant decrease in swimming distances at 2 and 5 DPT with no significant difference between uninjected and CRISPR animals.
source: Following SCI, there is a significant decrease in swimming distances at 2 and 5 DPT with no significant difference between uninjected and CRISPR animals (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by swimming test data shown in Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 10 DPT, the average swimming distance of uninjected tadpoles had recovered to a level not significantly different from pre-injury levels.
source: However, at 10 DPT, the average swimming distance of uninjected tadpoles had recovered to a level not significantly different from pre-injury levels.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by swimming test data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At 10 DPT, the average swimming distance of CRISPR tadpoles was significantly shorter than uninjected tadpoles.
source: In contrast, the average swimming distance of 10 DPT CRISPR tadpoles was significantly shorter (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by swimming test data shown in Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Animals with sham surgeries showed no significant changes in swimming distances compared to uninjected and uninjured tadpoles over time.
source: Animals with sham surgeries showed no significant changes in swimming distances compared to uninjected and uninjured tadpoles over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that spinal cord transection alone accounts for these behavioral differences.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by swimming test data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Horizontal sections of the spinal cords of uninjured 4M CRISPR-injected animals resembled those of uninjured animals with prominent and well-distinguished ventricular, mantle, and marginal zones.
source: Horizontal sections of the spinal cords of uninjured 4M CRISPR-injected animals resembled those of uninjured animals with prominent and well-distinguished ventricular, mantle, and marginal zones (Figure 6B, F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B, F.

claim: After SCI, the length of the injury gap is initially similar for uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected tadpoles.
source: After SCI, the length of the injury gap is initially similar for uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected tadpoles (Figure 6C, G, J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C, G, J.

claim: At 5 DPT, the first axonal bridges seem to form and connect the rostral and caudal stumps in the uninjected animals, which is delayed until 10 DPT in the CRISPR tadpoles.
source: However, at 5 DPT, the first axonal bridges seem to form and connect the rostral and caudal stumps in the uninjected animals, which is delayed until 10 DPT in the CRISPR tadpoles (Figure 6D, E, H, I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D, E, H, I.

claim: The injury gap at 5- and 10-DPT in 4M CRISPR-injected remained significantly larger than in uninjected embryos.
source: Moreover, while the injury gap decreased over time in both uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected tadpoles, the injury gap at 5- and 10-DPT in 4M CRISPR-injected remained significantly larger than in uninjected embryos, indicating a delay in regenerative closure (Figure 6D, E, H, I, J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D, E, H, I, J.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportion of EdU+ cells between uninjured uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected animals.
source: There was no significant difference between uninjured uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected animals (Figure 7 A1, B1, A2, B, I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 7 A1, B1, A2, B, I.

claim: In response to SCI, a significant increase in the proportion of EdU+ cells was observed in uninjected tadpoles at 2- and 5-DPT, which returned to pre-injury levels at 10 DPT.
source: In response to SCI, then a significant increase in the proportion of EdU+ cells was observed in uninjected tadpoles at 2- and 5-DPT, which returned to pre-injury levels at 10 DPT (Figure 7A1–H, I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 7A1-H, I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sham-operated animals showed no significant changes in EdU+ cells over time.
source: Sham-operated animals showed no significant changes in EdU+ cells over time (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), indicating that these changes occur only after spinal cord transection.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant change in the proportion of EdU+ cells in the 4M CRISPR-injected tadpoles after SCI.
source: In contrast, there was no significant change in the proportion of EdU+ cells in the 4M CRISPR-injected tadpoles after SCI (Figure 7A2–H2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 7A2-H2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution of Sox2+ cells in the ventricular zone was similar, and there was no significant difference between uninjured uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected animals.
source: Again, the distribution of Sox2+ cells in the ventricular zone was similar, and there was no significant difference between uninjured uninjected and 4M CRISPR-injected animals (Figure 8 A1, B1, A2, B2, I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Sox2 staining data shown in Figure 8 A1, B1, A2, B2, I.

claim: In uninjected tadpoles at 2 and 5 DPT, an increase in Sox2+ cell numbers was observed rostral to the injury site of the transected spinal cord.
source: In uninjected tadpoles at 2 and 5 DPT, we observed an increase in Sox2+ cell numbers rostral to the injury site of the transected spinal cord (Figure 8C1–F1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Sox2 staining data shown in Figure 8C1-F1.

claim: Near the injury, Sox2+ cells were reduced (particularly at 2 DPT) in uninjected tadpoles.

claim: The downregulation of Marcks and Marcksl1 in postmetamorphic froglets may be one of the factors preventing spinal cord regeneration in adults.
source: Our findings that Marcks and Marcksl1 are required for proper regeneration of the spinal cord after injury suggest that the downregulation of both proteins in postmetamorphic froglets (Kshirsagar, 2020) may be one of the factors preventing spinal cord regeneration in adults.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings that Marcks and Marcksl1 are required for regeneration and that they are downregulated in non-regenerative froglets.

claim: Marcks- and Marcksl1-immunopositive immune cells that infiltrate the injury site may contribute to the regeneration-promoting effects of these proteins.
source: However, since both proteins are known to be expressed in macrophages and other immune cells and can modulate the inflammatory response (Carballo et al., 1999; El Amri et al., 2018; Zhou and Li, 2000), Marcks- and Marcksl1-immunopositive immune cells that infiltrate the injury site may also contribute to the regeneration-promoting effects of these proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on known functions of these proteins in immune cells and their presence at the injury site.

claim: Unphosphorylated, membrane-bound Marcks promotes neurite outgrowth and progenitor proliferation via PIP2-dependent activation of phospholipid signaling.
source: Taken together with our findings that enhancement of PIP2 synthesis and PLC signaling as well as inhibition of PKC is also able to partially rescue the effects of Marcks and Marcksl1 loss of function during spinal cord development, this is compatible with a model in which unphosphorylated, membrane-bound Marcks promotes neurite outgrowth and progenitor proliferation via PIP2-dependent activation of phospholipid signaling (Figure 9T).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the pharmacological rescue experiments and is supported by data shown in Figure 9T.
